s.d: Asiatic Rock dove: bird with a blue-gray color with a pinkish sheen to the neck feathers and a black tip on its tail; lives in large colonies and eats mainly seeds; courts, mates, and has nests several times a year; nests on rock ledges; Columba via; used as food and for sacrifices; regarded as swift, docile, and innocent
s.c: Though in English a relatively clear distinction is made between ‘doves’ (which have pointed tails) and ‘pigeons’ (which have square off tails), there seems to be no such distinction in the use of περιστερά and τρυγών in the Greek of the New Testament.|There are, however, certain problems involved in the connotations of terms relating to pigeons or doves. According to ancient zoology, the dove was thought to have no bile, and consequently, therefore, to be a very peaceful and clean bird. It thus became a symbol of Christian virtue and of gentleness (as in ⟦Matthew 10:16|Matthew 10:16⟧). In reality, however, doves and pigeons are quite aggressive, and a group of pigeons are frequently known to peck an injured bird to death. Therefore, in some societies pigeons or doves are not regarded as gentle or peaceful, but rather as wicked and harmful. In fact, in some cultures doves are thought to be symbols of death and of evil. Under such circumstances it is important, therefore, to have some marginal note so as to indicate clearly the symbolic significance of such birds in biblical contexts.

s.d: to cut off the foreskin of the male genital organ as a religious rite involving consecration and ethnic identification
s.c: In the case of societies which practice circumcision, there is normally a perfectly satisfactory term to designate this type of operation, though it may not have any religious significance but only be a part of puberty ritual. For societies which do not practice circumcision or are not well acquainted with such a practice, a term which specifically describes the operation may be both offensive and vulgar. It may therefore be necessary to use a borrowing or to employ a somewhat obscure term such as ‘to cut around’ and then to explain the specific meaning of the term or phrase in a glossary.|Even in the case of societies which practice circumcision, there may be problems in comprehension of the significance of such an act, and these difficulties may require marginal notes. If, for example, a society practices circumcision only in connection with puberty rites, it may seem inexplicable that Jesus would have been circumcised on the eighth day after his birth (⟦Luke 2:21|Luke 2:21⟧). In many societies such an act would seem to be either a deed of extreme cruelty to a baby or a sign of mature sexuality in an infant.

any kind of bird, wild or domestic
s.c: All languages have at least some terms for birds, but there may be no generic term which identifies birds while excluding all other creatures which fly. For example, in some languages a term which includes all kinds of birds also includes flying insects and bats. However, since in most instances such a term has birds as its primary reference, it can usually be employed in contexts in which birds are more or less readily identified by other expressions in the passage. In other languages generic terms for birds may identify only certain classes of birds, for example, birds of prey, water birds, and birds of the forest.

In some languages the equivalent expression is ‘birds of the trees’ or ‘birds of the winds.’

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: bedrock (possibly covered with a thin layer of soil), rocky crags, or mountain ledges, in contrast with separate pieces of rock normally referred to as {L:λίθος<SDBG:λίθος:000000>}[a] (see {D:2.23}){N:001}
s.c: ὁμοιωθήσεται ἀνδρὶ φρονίμῳ, ὅστις ᾠκοδόμησεν αὐτοῦ τὴν οἰκίαν ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν ‘he is like a wise man who built his house on bedrock’ ⟦Matthew 7:24|Matthew 7:24⟧; ἔθηκεν αὐτὸν ἐν μνημείῳ ὅ ἦν λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας ‘they then put him in a grave which had been hewn from rock’ ⟦Mark 15:46|Mark 15:46⟧; λέγουσιν τοῖς ὄρεσιν καὶ ταῖς πέτραις, Πέσετε ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς ‘they said to the mountains and to the rock cliffs, Fall on us’ ⟦Revelation 6:16|Revelation 6:16⟧. In these three contexts πέτρα must be translated in some languages by three quite different terms. Bedrock, that is to say, the rock which lies horizontally and often just below the surface, may be referred to by one term, while rock with an exposed face into which a tomb could be hewn would be quite different. Similarly, the rocks which would be called upon to fall upon people would be rendered by a term referring to ‘cliffs’ or ‘precipices.’|In ⟦Luke 8:6|Luke 8:6⟧ the term πέτρα in ἕτερον κατέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν ‘other (seed) fell on rocky ground’ refers to bedrock which may be covered with a thin layer of soil. One may translate such an expression as ‘thin ground over rock’ or ‘just a little soil on top of rock.’|In those passages which involve a play on words with the name Πέτρος ‘Peter,’ πέτρα refers to bedrock, that is to say, the rock on which a foundation may be placed.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the Greek name of the leader of the twelve apostles, who was also called Cephas and whose name was originally Simon

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: (derivative of {L:πέτρα<SDBG:πέτρα:000000>} ‘bedrock,’ {D:2.21}) a rocky substance or bedrock covered by a thin layer of earth

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: an evergreen aromatic plant used for seasoning
s.c: In the parallel passage (⟦Matthew 23:23|Matthew 23:23⟧) ἄνηθον ‘dill’ and κύμινον ‘cumin’ occur (see LN 3.24-LN 3.25).|In designating ‘rue’ as well as ἡδύοσμον 'mint', ἄνηθον ‘dill,’ and κύμινον ‘cumin,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called rue.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: a source of water flowing onto the surface or into a pool somewhat below ground level
s.c: πηγή spring differs from φρέαρ and πηγή well (see LN 7.57) in that a πηγή is normally a natural source of water, in contrast with φρέαρ and πηγή, which are dug and into which a πηγή may be said to flow.

s.d: deep constructions, often walled with stone, at the bottom of which was a pool of water
s.c: If there was a relatively ready flow of water, a well could very appropriately be called a πηγή 'spring,' LN 1.78 (and this may be the reason for πηγή. However, both terms are used interchangeably in certain contexts; compare, for example, πηγή in ⟦John 4:6|John 4:6⟧ and φρέαρ in ⟦John 4:11|John 4:11⟧, both referring to Jacob’s well at Sychar.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: (a set phrase, literally: fountain of blood) the loss of blood through menstrual bleeding{N:001}
s.g: loss of blood; menstrual flow; bleeding

s.d: to set up or erect a construction, often used in connection with tents
s.g: to set up; to erect; to put up

s.dp: Artifacts › Boats and Parts of Boats
s.d: a large plank at the stern of a ship used to direct its course
s.c: For some ships the rudder may have been simply a large steering paddle. For languages which have no technical term, a rudder may be described as ‘an instrument for steering the ship’ or ‘an instrument for making the ship go the way one wants it to go.’

s.d: an interrogative of large size

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: pertaining to a correlative degree of high status

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: moistened earth of a clay consistency
s.c: πηλός contrasts with βόρβορος ‘watery mud’ (LN 2.17) and refers to moist earth with a consistency of clay. It may be translated in some languages as ‘sticky soil’ or ‘clay-like mud’ or ‘moist dirt.’|In ⟦Romans 9:21|Romans 9:21⟧ (ἢ οὐκ ἔχει ἐξουσίαν ὁ κεραμεὺς τοῦ πηλοῦ ‘or doesn’t the man who makes the pots have the right to use the clay as he wishes’) the reference is specifically to potter’s clay. The meaning of πηλός, therefore, may be defined as any kind of moist earth with clay consistency. πηλός includes the area of meaning of κέραμος ‘potter’s clay’ (a meaning not occurring in the NT).|Since pottery is so widely known throughout the world, there is normally no difficulty in obtaining a term which refers to potter’s clay. Even when the making of pottery is not known, it is usually possible to obtain a satisfactory term for such clay, for example, ‘mud that can be molded’ or ‘mud for shaping pots.’

s.d: a bag used by travellers (or beggars) to carry possessions
s.c: It is possible that in ⟦Matthew 10:10|Matthew 10:10⟧ (and parallel passages) the reference is specifically to a ‘beggar’s bag’ used to collect food or money.

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › Specific Measures of Length
s.d: traditionally the distance from the elbow to the end of the fingers, about eighteen inches or one-half meter
s.c: The interpretation of πῆχυς in ⟦Matthew 6:27|Matthew 6:27⟧ as a measurement of stature rather than length of life may be justified as an instance of literary hyperbole or exaggeration. Most modern translations, however, interpret πῆχυς in this context as a reference to length of life rather than as a measurement of height (see discussion under ἡλικία in LN 67.151).

s.d: to take hold of firmly and with a considerable measure of force
s.g: to take hold of; to seize; to catch; to grasp firmly

s.dp: Control, Rule › Seize, Take into Custody
s.d: to take a person into custody for alleged illegal activity
to press down, in order to make more compact
plausible, but false, speech resulting from the use of well-constructed, probable arguments

s.dp: Features of Objects › Sweet, Bitter, Tasteless
s.d: to cause something to become bitter

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hate, Hateful
s.d: (derivative of {L:πικρία<SDBG:πικρία:000001>}[b] ‘bitterness,’ {D:88.201}) to have bitter resentment or hatred toward someone else
s.g: to be embittered; to have bitter hate

s.dp: Features of Objects › Sweet, Bitter, Tasteless
s.d: with a bitter taste (occurring only in the idiom χολὴ πικρίας)
s.c: As a part of the idiom εἰς χολὴν πικρίας εἰμί, πικρίας is to be understood in a literal sense but the idiom as such means to be particularly envious or resentful of someone (see LN 88.166).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hate, Hateful
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:πικρία<SDBG:πικρία:000000>}[a] ‘bitter taste,’ {D:79.40}) a state of sharp, intense resentment or hate

s.dp: Features of Objects › Sweet, Bitter, Tasteless
s.d: pertaining to being bitter or pungent

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Resentful, Hold a Grudge Against
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:πικρός<SDBG:πικρός:000000>}[a] ‘bitter,’ {D:79.41}) pertaining to feeling resentful
pertaining to feeling mental agony

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a procurator of Judea who gave the order for the crucifixion of Jesus

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: to be sick with a fever
s.c: Though in a number of languages one can say ‘a person has a fever,’ in some languages the reverse expression is used, for example, ‘the fever has a person.’ Similarly, instead of saying ‘a person has a disease,’ it is ‘the disease which grabs a person.’ One may often speak of a fever as ‘to become hot’ or ‘to burn’ or ‘to be sick with burning.’|It is also possible to understand πίμπρημι in ⟦Acts 28:6|Acts 28:6⟧ as a process of swelling up (see LN 23.163).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.c: It is also possible to understand πίμπρημι in ⟦Acts 28:6|Acts 28:6⟧ as being sick with a fever (see LN 23.159).

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
s.d: a small writing tablet (normally made of wood)
a relatively flat, large dish; made of baked clay or metal

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to consume liquids, particularly water and wine
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between drinking water and drinking alcoholic beverages. Still other terms may be employed in speaking of drinking soups or broths.

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:πίνω<SDBG:πίνω:000000>}[a] ‘to drink,’ {D:23.34}) the action of a material which soaks up a liquid
s.c: Instead of speaking about ‘the ground absorbing the rain’ or ‘… drinking up the rain,’ it is often more natural to describe the event as ‘the rain disappearing into the ground’ or ‘the rain flowing into the ground.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to drink a cup) to undergo a trying, difficult experience
s.g: to undergo a difficult experience; to drink the cup; to suffer
s.c: In a number of languages it is not possible to use the phrase ‘to drink the cup,’ since this will almost inevitably refer to the drinking of a poison cup as a means of proving innocence in an ordeal. Even if one uses a literal rendering of the idiom ‘to drink the cup,’ it is usually necessary to have some explanation as to the significance of the idiom.

s.d: a nutritionally rich, fatty quality
s.c: The text of ⟦Romans 11:17|Romans 11:17⟧ is strange, for literally it reads ‘of the root of the richness.’ As may be easily understood, a number of scribal variations occur in different manuscripts.|Since the reference in ⟦Romans 11:17|Romans 11:17⟧ is to the olive tree, the fruit of which produces so much oil, one can readily understand the basis for the extension of meaning. Some translations render πιότης simply as ‘sap’ (New English Bible), while others abandon completely the figure of speech, for example, TEV which has “you share the strong spiritual life.”|For another treatment of πιότης in ⟦Romans 11:17|Romans 11:17⟧, see LN 65.7.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:πιότης<SDBG:πιότης:000000>}[a] ‘fatness,’ {D:3.59}) a rich, valuable substance
s.c: For another interpretation of πιότης in ⟦Romans 11:17|Romans 11:17⟧, see LN 3.59.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Sell, Buy, Price
s.d: to dispose of property or provide services in exchange for money or other valuable considerations
s.c: πιπράσκω and ἀποδίδομαι (ἀποδίδωμι) may also be used to refer to selling a person into slavery. Note, for example, πιπράσκω in ⟦Matthew 18:25|Matthew 18:25⟧ (ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος πραθῆναι ‘his master ordered him to be sold as a slave’) and ἀποδίδομαι in ⟦Acts 7:9|Acts 7:9⟧ (οἱ πατριάρχαι ζηλώσαντες τὸν Ἰωσὴφ ἀπέδοντο εἰς Αἴγυπτον ‘the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him to be a slave in Egypt’).|In a number of languages, however, it may be important to use a distinctive term for selling a person into slavery. In fact, it may be necessary to describe the event rather explicitly, for example, ‘to receive money for handing a person over to someone else to be a slave.’|In ⟦Romans 7:14|Romans 7:14⟧ πιπράσκω is used figuratively in the phrase πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ‘sold as a slave to sin,’ in the sense that sin is personified as the master.

s.d: to fall from one level to another{N:001}
to fall from a standing or upright position down to the ground or surface{N:001}

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Prostrate as an Act of Reverence or Supplication
s.d: to prostrate oneself before someone, implying supplication{N:002}
s.g: to prostrate oneself before; to fall down before
s.c: A strictly literal translation of προσπίπτω or πίπτω, namely, to fall down before, can be entirely misleading in that it may suggest an accident caused by stumbling or tripping. It may therefore be necessary in a number of languages to translate to bow down low before or to bow down to the ground before.

s.d: to suffer or experience destruction
s.g: to experience destruction; to be destroyed

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:πίπτω<SDBG:πίπτω:000000>}[a] ‘to fall,’ {D:15.118}) to fall down, as a euphemistic expression for a violent death
s.c: It is rare that one can employ a literal meaning of πίπτω as a euphemistic expression for ‘dying,’ since receptors are too likely to understand ‘to fall’ in a purely literal sense.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:πίπτω<SDBG:πίπτω:000000>}[a] ‘to fall,’ {D:15.118}) to cease, with the possible implication of failure
s.g: to stop; to cease; to fail
s.c: For another interpretation of πίπτω in ⟦1 Corinthians 13:8|1 Corinthians 13:8⟧, see LN 75.7.

s.d: to happen suddenly to, with the connotation of something bad and adverse
s.g: to happen to; to fall upon
s.c: In this particular context it may be necessary to be somewhat more specific concerning the blindness that Elymas experienced. For example, one may render this expression as ‘suddenly a dark mist covered his eyes’ or ‘suddenly the eyes of Elymas became dark and misty’ (see LN 24.40).

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: to change for the worse, with emphasis upon extent and suddenness
to cease to exist in a particular post or position
s.g: to cease; to come to an end; to fall

s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:πίπτω<SDBG:πίπτω:000000>}[a] ‘to fall,’ {D:15.118}) to become inadequate for some function
s.c: For another interpretation of πίπτω in ⟦1 Corinthians 13:8|1 Corinthians 13:8⟧, see LN 68.49.

s.d: to experience somewhat suddenly that which is difficult or bad
s.g: to come to experience; to experience; to encounter; to be beset by

s.dp: Think › To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the lot falls upon someone) the process of choosing, with the probable implication of discerning God’s will in this manner
s.g: to choose by lot; to select by lot
s.c: In some societies the closest natural equivalents of deciding by lot are procedures involving ‘drawing straws’ or ‘throwing dice’ or ‘throwing down sticks’ or ‘dropping pebbles.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to fall upon someone) to cause someone suffering or harm
s.g: to cause to suffer; to cause pain to
s.c: It is rare indeed that this idiom can ever be produced literally in other languages, though it may be possible to preserve some of the figurative impact by translating ‘nor will the heat of the sun ever cause them to suffer.’

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to his own master he stands or falls, probably a familiar adage) whether one maintains one’s status or relationship to a master depends on the masters judgment or evaluation
s.g: honor or disgrace depends on the person whom one serves

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judge, Condemn, Acquit
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to fall under judgment) to be condemned for acting contrary to laws and regulations
s.g: to be condemned; to suffer condemnation; to be judged guilty
s.c: In the context of ⟦James 5:12|James 5:12⟧ the condemnation refers to God’s judgment.

s.d: to fall together in a heap

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a region in central Asia Minor

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Πισιδία<SDBG:Πισιδία:000000>} ‘Pisidia,’ {D:93.552}) pertaining to Pisidia
